newsitem.title: FRANCE: European Parliament sees major reshuffles.
newsitem.headline: European Parliament sees major reshuffles.

text.p: The European Parliament, just emerging from three major reshuffles in less than a week, starts the ball rolling on Wednesday for further fundamental changes in January 1997.

On Monday, the anti-federalist Europe of Nations group officially ceased to exist when French member Anne Christine left for the right-wing Union for Europe group, leaving the EDN with only 17 members -- one short of the minimum needed to survive.
The same day, the first directly elected MEPs from Austria and Finland took their 37 seats in the parliament, swelling the ranks of its right-wing parties.

These changes come five days after the Liberal Party suffered a body blow when its eight Portuguese members -- the largest national group in the party -- defected to the mainly Christian Democrat EPP.

The next round of changes begins before the dust has even settled, as the EPP on Wednesday decides in effect who will take over from German Socialist Klaus Haensch as president of the parliament next January.

Jose Maria Gil-Robles, a legal official in the Spanish government in the time of General Franco, is tipped to be the front runner in a three-horse race between three of the EPP's parliamentary vice-presidents.
The other two EPP candidates are French lawyer Nicole Fontaine and the former Athens lawyer and journalist Georgios Anastassopoulos.

An agreement Between Parliament's two largest political groups, the 215-member Socialist Party (PES) and the 182-member EPP, ensures that the post of parliament president passes from PES to EPP and back every two and a half years.
The parliament's smaller parties are somewhat disgruntled with the arrangement and are talking of putting up a symbolic opposition candidate to the EPP's nominee for the "election" in January.
The name of the Radical group's French chairwoman, Catherine Lalumiere, was mentioned to Reuters as one possible choice.
At the same time as they elect their new president, MEPs will choose 14 new vice-presidents and 23 heads of committee.
At present the PES boasts five vice-presidents and the president among their number, while the EPP has six vice-presidents.
The next three largest political groups, the UPE, the Liberals and the United Left/Nordic Left all have one vice-president.
Or rather they did, until Liberal vice-president Antonio Capucho led the eight Portuguese members of the group into the EPP fold.
He will be seeking one of the EPP's vice-president posts, his Portuguese colleagues say.
How the race for the other vice-presidential seats lines up will become clearer in December.

The same goes for the leaderships of the parliamentary committees, though Socialist group sources are already predicting their British member Eddy Newman will be replaced as head of the petitions committee.
This is simply because British Socialists are already over-represented in positions of power, they say.
As well as the petitions committee, British Labour MEPs chair the Environment and Social Affairs Committees -- seen as more crucial posts to retain -- and hold the leadership of the PES itself.

After losing its eight Portuguese members, the Liberal group fears it may not be able to keep the chairmanship of the prestigious external economic relations committee, currently headed by former Belgian Finance Minister Willy de Clerq.
Some of the new posts should go to newcomers from the three new EU member states, Austria, Finland and Sweden, whose arrival has increased the number of MEPS from 567 to 626.
Their entry into Parliament has boosted the fortunes of the two largest parties (PES and EPP), the United Left/Nordic Left and the Greens, and swelled the ranks of non-aligned MEPs from 27 to 49.
The now defunct EDN and the Liberals are the groups who have fared least well since the last EP elections in July 1994.
There were 43 Liberals in the 567-member Parliament. After gaining and then losing nine members, the group still has 43 members, although the total number of MEPs has risen by 59.

That the number of non-aligned members practically doubled on November 11 is due mainly to the demise of the EDN and the arrival of six MEPs from Austrian nationalist Joerg Haider's Freedom Party (FPO), the biggest far-right grouping in Europe.

Ironically, after officially denying rumours they had tried to keep their party alive by inviting the Freedom Party into their fold, the members of the erstwhile EDN, who include British billionaire Sir James Goldsmith, now find themselves on the same benches as Haidar and his collegues.
The six FPO members have said they will work with other like-minded groups in the parliament to push for a review of the Maastricht Treaty.

Goldsmith, who amassed a fortune as an entrepreneur, wants a referendum on Britain's future in Europe and plans to put forward about 600 candidates for his Referendum Party at the British general election next year.
